newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: OUB says profit growth may slow 1997.
newsitem.headline: OUB says profit growth may slow 1997.

text.p: Overseas Union Bank Ltd may see its profit growth slow in 1997 due to the current economic slowdown in Singapore, president and chief executive officer Peter Seah said on Friday.

But Seah said OUB, one of Singapore's big four banks with a net profit of Singapore $259.33 in 1995, could be partly insulated from any slowdown by the fact that about a third of its income came from outside Singapore.
"I would say 1997 may well be a year with possibly a slower profit growth," Seah told Reuters in an interview.

"The economic slowdown in Singapore would probably translate into slower demand for credit. I think probably the area where the greatest impact will be would likely be the area of housing loans, particularly in the second half of 1997," Seah added.
Singapore experienced rapid economic growth through the early 1990s with a jump of 8.8 percent in its gross domestic product (GDP) in 1995.

But the recent slump in the global electronics industry, on which the city-state relies for the consumption of almost half of its industrial production and 60 percent of its non-oil exports, has slowed growth this year.
Economists predict Singapore's economic growth will average slightly over seven percent for 1996 as a whole.
However, Seah said OUB should be helped by the strength of its overseas income and treasury operations.

"We feel that OUB will also be better buffered by the fact that more than 30 percent of our income comes from outside of Singapore and that doesn't even include income from our treasury operations," Seah said. "Treasury operations are not dependent on economic growth in Singapore."
Seah said the bank expected another very good year for Malaysia in 1997.
"And we expect all the other overseas centres to be doing better, perhaps with the exception of Hong Kong, where with some degree of uncertainty in 1997 we may see a more flat performance," he said.
Seah said profits in 1997 could be helped by an improvement in the performance of Asian stockmarkets.

"Our markets have been somewhat lacklustre for quite a while already and the Dow (Jones Industrial index of U.S. stocks) is at record highs. So it would not be unreasonable to expect some shifting of funds back into the markets in this part of the world which would mean better stockbroking income," he said.

"So I expect 1997 to be a reasonable year. I am not pessimistic over 1997 and I expect that because of the strength of our international overseas operations, we will probably be able to do comparatively better than our competitors."
